base_prompt: A website asks users to confirm a destructive action twice. Discuss when this helps and when repeated confirmation becomes ineffective. Aim for about 200 words.
text: A second confirmation can help when the action is genuinely irreversible, costly, or likely to be triggered accidentally, such as permanently deleting an account, erasing important data, cancelling a paid service, or publishing sensitive information. It creates a brief pause in which users can recognize a mistaken click, reconsider consequences, or notice that they selected the wrong item. The extra step is especially useful when the first action may occur through a crowded interface, keyboard shortcut, or ambiguous control. Its effectiveness depends on being meaningful: the confirmation should clearly state what will happen, identify the affected item, and offer a safe way to cancel. However, repeated confirmations quickly become ineffective when they appear for routine, low-risk actions or use generic wording that users learn to dismiss automatically. If people encounter the same warning constantly, they develop “click-through” behavior and confirm without reading, much like ignoring cookie banners or software prompts. Multiple identical dialogs can also frustrate users and slow legitimate work without improving safety. Designers should therefore reserve double confirmation for exceptional, high-impact actions, make the warning specific and comprehensible, and consider alternatives such as an undo period, soft deletion, backup, or requiring a deliberate typed phrase for the most serious cases.
